title: Creating an Appetite for Feedback
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article lays out a three-step method for leaders who want their own team members to actively seek feedback: ask for feedback themselves first, visibly act on what they receive, and then close the loop by telling the person what impact their input had. It offers better alternatives to vague questions like 'how did I do,' recommending specific prompts that invite genuine, actionable responses. The piece argues the final step, reporting back on impact, is what actually creates appetite for future feedback, since it demonstrates the exchange is mutual rather than one-directional.

Team members are said to reserve their own feedback until a leader has earned it through this process.
quotes: Leaders who want team members to seek feedback need to do three things: ask for feedback, act on it, and tell the giver when it has had an impact.
Try asking a better question than “How did I do?” — a phrase that can come across as fishing for a compliment.
Leaders show others that their feedback is valuable when they act on it.
Good leaders go a step further and describe how important the suggestion was.
As a rule, team members won’t seek feedback from a leader until they have earned it. Be the kind of leader who makes others hungry for input.
